item.title: A phase-field model of viscous surfaces in fluids
item.description: arXiv:2611.13902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Viscous surfaces play a crucial role in biological and industrial multiphase flows, yet their simulation remains challenging due to complex rheology and topological changes. We present a thermodynamically consistent phase-field model for viscous surfaces in incompressible Navier-Stokes fluids, incorporating surface shear and dilatational viscosities via the Boussinesq-Scriven constitutive law. The diffuse-interface formulation is derived from a sharp-interface model and rigorously validated through matched asymptotic analysis, confirming recovery of the correct sharp-interface limit. We develop an unconditionally energy-dissipative time discretization, ensuring numerical stability. The model is validated through a quantitative benchmark against analytical solutions for surface flows on a rigid sphere, and a simulation of vesicle fusion showing preservation of energy dissipation across topological transitions. These results demonstrate that the framework enables robust, physically consistent simulations of complex surface dynamics, including large deformations and topological changes, without explicit surface tracking.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Kloppe, Sebastian Aland

item.title: Rheology of Parametric Odd Materials
item.description: arXiv:2611.13969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The design and control of rheological properties in active systems are crucial for developing functional materials with novel properties. While significant attention has been devoted to odd viscosity and odd elasticity, comprehensive odd rheological models remain scarce. Here, we introduce and characterise a platform-agnostic odd viscoelastic material, where complex responses arise from parametric control of internal rotational degrees of freedom and are triggered by coupling between normal and shear stresses. Such control can be achieved through either parametric driving or a parametric nonlinear feedback. We further show that this coupling can induce rotation-driven fluidisation, transitioning the material from an elasticity-dominated to a viscosity-dominated regime. Lastly, we show that the interplay between odd and even sectors enhances the nonlinear material response under large-amplitude oscillatory shear (LAOS). The findings outline a route to Floquet-engineered metafluids with programmable, non-reciprocal rheology.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Cosme, Maziyar Jalaal

item.title: Analytic Two-Radius Model for the Zero-Shear and High-Frequency Viscosity of Colloidal Suspensions
item.description: arXiv:2611.13982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nearly hard-sphere colloids are stabilized by short-range repulsions that set their effective size and equilibrium microstructure. Their hydrodynamic interactions, in contrast, are set by the no-slip surface. Since these two do not necessarily coincide, there are potentially two effective radii that control their dynamics in different ways. Yet it is commonplace to model and analyze such suspensions with a single effective radius, which merges these different physics. Two-radius models, in which a hard, solvent-permeable shell surrounds a no-slip core, have been proposed to improve the description of these suspensions. Their rheology is known exactly at pair level, but at higher concentrations their zero-shear viscosity has been obtained only with semi-empirical expressions, which do not recover the exact pair result. Here, we close this gap with a theory for the zero-shear and high-frequency viscosity of these two-radius models. By keeping pairs out of near contact, the shell lowers the high-frequency viscosity, as our Stokesian dynamics simulations confirm, and shifts the zero-shear viscosity from hydrodynamic toward thermodynamic stress. We apply our theory to experiments on charge- and sterically stabilized colloids from the literature and find that it accurately describes the measured viscosities. We discuss the benefits of fitting data to a two-radius model compared to a single-radius one. To facilitate this fitting in future work, closed-form expressions are provided that cover the full range of shell thicknesses and volume fractions.
item.dc:creator: Dimos Aslanis, Joost de Graaf

item.title: And yet it moves - or does it? Spurious drifts at equilibrium
item.description: arXiv:2611.14089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When diffusion depends on the state of a system, the drift measured from its trajectories contains a spurious part unrelated to forces. At equilibrium, particles can then appear to sediment, repel each other, even rotate - the same way whether the movie is played forward or backward. Drifts are conditional averages, not currents: they carry meaning only together with a consistently inferred diffusion tensor. Paired with the wrong one, they make passive particles look active. I show how to infer spurious drifts from trajectory moments alone, enabling thermodynamically consistent inference.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Ronceray

item.title: Mechanical pairing and self-assembled chains of non-convex granular rotors
item.description: arXiv:2611.14120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally and numerically demonstrate the self-assembly of granular rotors into chain-like structures. The rotors are non-convex rigid bodies with rotational activity. We first investigate the interaction between two rotors and we establish an attractive interaction controlled by the ratio of the rotational activity to the noise and also dependent of the rotors geometry. We then show that the cohesive state between spinner pairs leads to robust chains that can be either initially set or spontaneously obtained by self-assembly.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Barois, Melanie Labiausse, Jean-Francois Boudet, Juho S. Lintuvuori, Hamid Kellay

item.title: Cohesive granular piles with controlled volume fraction
item.description: arXiv:2611.14128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experimental procedures involving wet granular media expose the sample to variation of its organization across different measurements, leading to non reproducible results. Rigorous control over the preparation process and a thorough understanding of the microstructure of the granular heap are key parameters to manage results dispersion from one experiment to an other. In this study, we present a protocol to prepare large samples of wet grains in a cylindrical container. Quantitative results are presented showing the effectiveness of the protocol regarding : the accessibility of different granular materials with different volume fraction $\phi_0$ and the reproducibility of this said density obtained experimentally in the same experimental conditions. In addition, X-ray scans were performed using a micro-CT scanner to dive into the microstructure of the carefully prepared piles. Results show a small variation between the bulk density $\phi_0$ and the local one $\phi$, underlining the homogeneity in the samples. On top of that, several scans made in the same medium at different heights confirm the homogeneity across a given sample.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Jodlowski, Marie-Julie Dalbe, Nicolas Vandenberghe

item.title: Banding instabilities in poroelastic media under flow-driven compaction
item.description: arXiv:2611.14235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When cross-linked poroelastic media are subjected to a hydrostatic pressure difference, they compact, remaining fully swollen on their uppermost surface and becoming increasingly compressed with depth. A critical unexplored effect of cross-linking and resistance to shear deformation is investigated, which is not seen in classical models of poroelastic media treated as free elastic spheres, and resists the kind of compressive compaction that characterises these systems. Eventually, a steady-state profile dependent on osmotic, shear and transport properties is reached, supporting a uniform interstitial flow wherein the medium acts like a passive filter. In this paper, we show how these steady-state profiles are not necessarily stable, and propose a mechanism for the formation of instabilities, wherein some regions of the medium swell and others compact, forming distinctive horizontal or vertical banding patterns. In the latter case, these bands appear qualitatively to be higher-permeability conduits or channels, similar to wormholes or tunnels seen in granular media. It is possible to quantify the effect of changing the pressure head on the growth rate of instabilities and the separation lengthscale in this channelisation case, and how material properties like shear stiffness and dependence of permeability on porosity affect the dynamics of instability. Critically, it is shown that these instabilities are a fluid-mechanical effect, with an entirely new mechanism based on the porosity--permeability relationship and not on elastic effects. With an understanding of these mechanisms, we can derive insight into channelisation in poroelastic systems in geophysics, human biology and industry.
item.dc:creator: Joseph J. Webber

item.title: Chemotactic Horizons Regulate Threshold Dynamics in the Biological Carbon Pump
item.description: arXiv:2611.13165v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Microbial encounters with sinking marine snow regulate organic carbon remineralization, acting as a critical knob in the ocean's biological carbon pump. Yet how the vast diversity of microbes in the open ocean respond to natural chemotactic cues coupling sedimentation-induced flow to microbial encounters in the ocean remains unresolved. Here we report shipboard measurements of microbial motility around freshly collected marine snow under imposed flows spanning ecologically relevant sinking speeds. Via high resolution single cell tracking at sea, we map a highly diverse repertoire of microbial motility, including rapid switching between motile and non-motile states. We identify a chemotactic horizon from measured reorientation towards chemical gradients, defining a spatial region around an aggregate within which chemotactic alignment overcomes flow-induced rotation due to sedimentation. This interplay produces a non-monotonic dependence of encounter rates on aggregate sinking speed, with a peak at 14.4 m/day followed by a sharp decline beyond 78.1 m/day, with a tracer-like regime at high effective sinking speeds. We incorporate the measured encounter rates into a kinetic transport equation in position-velocity phase space, with an effective nonlinear damping arising from velocity-dependent remineralization. The resulting particle dynamics reveal a threshold-induced separatrix dividing overdamped and ballistic microbial populations, leading to velocity segregation. Our study connects direct measurements of microbial motility and sedimentation-induced flow to the emergent phase-space for fate of marine snow in the biological pump, establishing a quantitative multiscale framework for investigating ocean carbon export.
item.dc:creator: Rahul Chajwa, Manu Prakash

item.title: A new representation of effective diffusion in fluctuating periodic potentials through stochastic duality
item.description: arXiv:2611.13526v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We revisit the classical problem of effective diffusion in fluctuating periodic force fields by combining homogenization with stochastic duality. We consider a specific class of fluctuations in which the internal state of the force field is independently redrawn from a fixed distribution at Poisson-distributed times. In the homogenization framework, the effective diffusion coefficient \(D_{\rm eff}\) is expressed in terms of a corrector function satisfying a backward Kolmogorov equation. For the redraw dynamics considered here, the equation governing the spatial derivative of the corrector can be reinterpreted as the stationary forward equation of a dual system obtained by reversing the force field, \(F\to-F\). This relation eliminates the corrector and yields a representation of \(D_{\rm eff}\) entirely in terms of stationary densities and probability currents of the physical and dual systems. We further introduce an auxiliary function \(Q(x)\) whose spatial variation is determined by the stationary current. When this current vanishes, \(Q(x)\) becomes independent of position and the effective diffusion coefficient reduces to the local relation \( D_{\rm eff}=L^2Q. \) This result generalizes the classical Lifson--Jackson relation to fluctuating periodic force fields. We verify the theory using analytical calculations, numerical solutions of the stationary equations, and direct simulations of the long-time particle displacement, including a driven system with nonzero stationary current.
item.dc:creator: Derek Frydel

item.title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid
item.description: arXiv:2611.14104v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work identified spatially localised midplane stress structures as the building blocks of chaotic behaviour in pressure-driven parallel shear flows of viscoelastic fluids. Such coherent structures are thought to originate from a linear centre-mode instability of the laminar state. In the absence of inertia, however, the Oldroyd-B and FENE-P constitutive models predict that this instability is confined to ultra-dilute polymer solutions and very large Weissenberg numbers in channel flow, while no purely elastic instability has been reported in pipe flow. Here, we study numerically the linear stability of channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) fluid and find a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both geometries across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers. Since the sPTT and FENE-P models have identical steady rheology and laminar profiles, their contrasting predictions indicate that the existence of the centre-mode instability is governed by the transient rheological response of the fluid. Our results suggest that the purely elastic centre-mode instability should be observable under realistic flow conditions. They also offer a means of discriminating between constitutive models.
item.dc:creator: Calum S. Skene, Jeffrey S. Oishi, Keaton J. Burns, Moritz Linkmann, Geoffrey M. Vasil, Alexander Morozov

item.title: Geometric regulation of stress-limited growth on surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.14159v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We analyze a model for microbial communities growing on surfaces in which individual growth is inhibited by collective growth-induced pressure. Asymptotic and numerical solutions on the sphere and homogenization of periodic surfaces show surface geometry can be tuned to either slow or accelerate growth. We use these insights to identify classes of surfaces for which the growth rate can be made arbitrarily small or arbitrarily close to the stress-free growth rate. These results show stress-sensing is coupled to surface curvature and topography at scales much larger than the individual, and provide design principles for controlling the growth of stress-sensitive microbial communities.
item.dc:creator: Scott Weady

item.title: From Distribution of Extremes With Degradation to the Stress Redundancy Principle
item.description: arXiv:2611.14375v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How a degradation source affects the statistics of the first among many identical independent stochastic particles to successfully reach a narrow target remains unclear. Here, we investigate the impact of degradation on the distributions of first-passage times and exit locations by exploiting the time-dependent fluxes associated with the corresponding Fokker-Planck equation. We also compute the escape probability by solving a mixed boundary value problem. In the large initial population $N_0$ limit, we derive an asymptotic formula for the mean first passage time associated with the fastest particle, revealing how the killing field modifies the classical $1/\log(N_0)$ scaling. However, when considering the population size at the time of the first exit, we obtain a specific dependency with respect to degradation, a phenomenon that we call the stress redundancy principle. For a degradation field restricted to a narrow subregion, we use an optimal control approach to derive the optimal trajectory where the fastest escape particles will be concentrated: interestingly, we report here that the optimal trajectories avoid the degradation area depending on killing intensity. Finally, we obtain analytical expressions for the distribution of first exit points along a narrow absorbing arc in two-dimensional regular domains. In addition, for a killing subregion tangent to the target boundary, our computations reveal how geometrical parameters influence the exit distribution. In summary, a killing source can significantly affect the statistics of the fastest diffusing particles, relevant for defining cellular and molecular time scales.
item.dc:creator: Fr\'ed\'eric Paquin-Lefebvre, \'Elisa Delbreil, David Holcman

item.title: The active chiral random walk
item.description: arXiv:2611.14446v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a minimal and intuitive lattice model for an active chiral particle which exhibits persistence, reversal, and chirality in its dynamics. It is fully defined by a small set of microscopic parameters that provide transparent control over the resulting dynamics. By coarse-graining, we extract continuum equations and closed-form expressions for the velocity autocorrelation, off-diagonal directional correlation, mean-squared displacement, and long-time diffusion and odd diffusion coefficients. The complex parameter $\lambda=q_p+\mathrm{i}q_c$ thereby encodes the microscopic information on persistence ($q_p$) and chirality ($q_c$) of the walker. In a weak-turning limit, microscopically realized by infrequent reorientation events, the continuum description can be mapped onto well-established models of active matter. Outside this limit the discrete model exhibits finite-step dynamics, such as anti-persistent motion, that are not captured by a smooth angular-diffusion description. The model therefore provides a compact, exactly solvable, and readily tunable framework in which a small number of transparent microscopic parameters control chiral active transport.
item.dc:creator: Nir Sherf, Joshua Uhlig, Jan W\'ojcik, Ralf Metzler, Yael Roichman, Erik Kalz

item.title: Crowding and confinement of mesoscale swimmers in living droplets
item.description: arXiv:2509.20005v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Droplets encapsulating active or living matter provide controllable platforms for studying collective dynamics and active interfacial actuation. However, prior work has largely focused on quasi-2D confinement, microscopic swimmers, or externally driven, non-living droplets. Here, we introduce living droplets internally activated by tens of enclosed mesoscale swimmers to study crowding and confinement in 3D with swimmer sizes comparable to the droplet radius. In large droplets with few swimmers, the droplet oscillation frequencies collapse onto the classical sessile-drop frequency-volume scaling. By increasing the number of swimmers or decreasing the droplet size, crowding and confinement alter the droplet oscillation frequencies and amplitudes as many-body or swimmer-droplet interactions start dominating. We develop a scaling-law framework linking the oscillation amplitude to swimmer speed through collision probability and momentum transfer, enabling indirect 3D velocimetry in the opaque, crowded droplets. Complementary quasi-2D experiments with direct tracking reveal dimensionality-dependent crowding effects, which we successfully describe with a kinetic theory-based model. We show distinct crossovers and strong-crowding asymptotic scalings of the swimmer speed with the dimensionless swimmer density, $U_{\mathrm{crowd}}\sim(N^{\ast})^{-1}$ in 3D and $U_{\mathrm{crowd}}\sim(N^{\ast})^{-1/2}$ in quasi-2D. Our results connect mesoswimmer encounter dynamics to macroscopic droplet mechanics and inform the design of bio-inspired micromachines, fluidic control, and sensing technologies.
item.dc:creator: L. Malik, N. Sharadhi, C. Pr\^echeur Llarena, M. Lamminm\"aki, R. A. Lara, V. Jokinen, M. Lisicki, M. Backholm

item.title: Mapping the limits of equilibrium in sheared granular liquid crystals
item.description: arXiv:2603.25252v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While elongated particles in viscous fluids follow Jeffery orbits, their dynamics in dense granular flows remain unresolved. We demonstrate that sheared, low friction granular rods do not follow these orbits, but instead reach a quasi-equilibrium state quantitatively described by classical liquid crystal theory, with collisions providing effective thermal noise. This quasi-equilibrium analogy breaks down at two limits: low aspect ratios, where the theory incorrectly predicts isotropy, and high inter-particle friction, which drives a transition from steric screening to frictional gearing. We map this far-from-equilibrium breakdown using a phenomenological effective Ericksen number, establishing the limits of thermal thermodynamic analogies in driven athermal matter.
item.dc:creator: Jacopo Bilotto, Martin Trulsson, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Molinari

item.title: Bubbles in highly porous media: Clogging and unclogging at constrictions
item.description: arXiv:2603.28511v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gas bubble transport through highly porous transport layers (PTLs) is a key process in electrochemical devices such as proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers, where bubbles generated at catalyst surfaces must migrate through complex porous networks. To understand this process, we focus on model systems, namely the motion of single, paired and multiple bubbles in capillaries and study these by combining analytical modeling, three-dimensional color-gradient lattice Boltzmann simulations, and X-ray radiography. For single bubbles, we derive an analytical expression for the critical Bond number separating passage from clogging and show that, in the low deformation regime, it accurately predicts this transition in circular capillaries. Extending the study to bubble pairs, we uncover additional clogging and unclogging pathways, including hydrodynamic unclogging driven by pressure buildup in the interbubble film, and coalescence-induced clogging and unclogging. By mapping our results as functions of confinement ratio and Bond number, we define distinct dynamical regimes that control bubble passage. Experiments on bubble chains rising through highly porous nickel foams confirm the predicted clogging and unclogging mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: J. M. P. Beunen, T. Lappan, P. Malgaretti, O. Aouane, K. Eckert, J. Harting

item.title: Kinetics of segregation of topologically-modified ring polymers in cylindrical confinement
item.description: arXiv:2604.26087v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In Escherichia coli (E. coli), entropic repulsion between the two daughter DNA ring polymers under cylindrical confinement is believed to be an important factor governing chromosomal segregation. The repulsion can be enhanced by topological modifications, i.e., by the introduction of internal loops at certain locations along the contour of the circular DNA. However, the effect of topological modifications on the rate of segregation of ring polymers remains unclear. Therefore, we systematically varied the number and the contour length of loops introduced at selected locations by crosslinking monomers. The appropriate crosslinking was motivated by observations that extruded loops are located mainly near the origin of replication (ori-proximal) region of the E. coli chromosome. This resulted in the chains becoming intrinsically anisotropic. Using Langevin dynamics simulations of these topologically modified bead-spring polymers, we calculated the time required for segregation under cylinder confinement. With certain caveats, we found that increasing the number of loops resulted in a decrease in the time of segregation. In line with past work, we propose that this is due to the increase in the entropic repulsion between the polymers upon increasing the number of loops. In addition to the number of loops, the contour length of the loops and the mutual orientation of the (anisotropic) chains in the initial configurations played a role in determining the time of segregation.
item.dc:creator: Harsh Doshi, Shreerang Pande, Sathish K. Sukumaran, Apratim Chatterji

item.title: Depletion Capture and Rayleigh--Onsager Dynamics in Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis
item.description: arXiv:2607.12766v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Receptor-mediated endocytosis requires a particle to approach a membrane in a crowded extracellular environment, form ligand-receptor bonds, and wrap the membrane against bending, tension, and cytoskeletal viscoelastic resistance. We develop a two-stage theory. The capture stage uses the exact ideal hard-sphere Asakura--Oosawa sphere-plane excluded-volume geometry. The wrapping stage combines a spherical-cap coordinate, a quadratic single-mode free energy, a standard linear solid with one internal strain variable, and a two-variable Rayleigh--Onsager (RO) gradient flow. The creep compliance is mapped exactly onto a long-time spring in parallel with a Maxwell branch, preserving both the creep retardation and stress relaxation times. The free energy is strictly convex by its Hessian convexity, and the linear wrapping system has two real negative eigenvalues and an explicit double-exponential solution. Two independent arguments establish strict monotonicity for positive initial drive: the irreducible Metzler structure with its positive semigroup and the interlacing of Laplace poles with positive velocity residues. The first-passage equation has a unique finite root below the unconstrained long-time limit. Normal-cone conditions specify the projected dynamics on $0\le x\le2$, and the projected system retains the Lyapunov inequality of the unconstrained gradient flow. From the same free energy we derive long-time adhesion thresholds, the threshold-minimizing radius, the finite-size window, and the critical cell modulus. The $95\%$ spherical-area criterion is treated as an operational near-complete threshold, with $90\%$, $95\%$, and $99\%$ compared. The capture analysis includes the exact overlap volume, depletion force, Carnahan--Starling pressure rescaling, Stokes approach time, and Brenner wall-drag correction.
item.dc:creator: Jinjie Liu, Zhongcan Ouyang, Hao Wu

item.title: Fundamental Relation between Conductance of Biomolecules and the Fukui Function
item.description: arXiv:2607.13309v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We derive the finite-temperature conductance of a molecule coupled to metallic leads using open-system time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT). Tracing out the phonon bath via Wick's theorem yields an exchange-symmetric collision integral that preserves Pauli exclusion. When internal thermalization is faster than lead escape, as holds in proteins with multifractal orbitals at the Anderson transition, the exchange-correlation kernel projects out of the slow Liouvillian mode, making conductance directly proportional to the finite-temperature Fukui function of conceptual DFT.
item.dc:creator: Gabor Vattay

item.title: Three-body corrections to the Brownian viscosity of hard spheres without hydrodynamic interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.24948v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For Brownian hard spheres without hydrodynamic interactions, we study the part of the contact stress produced by three-body correlations: the third-order coefficient of the zero-shear Brownian viscosity. Kirkwood superposition gives zero for this coefficient: three nonzero pair contributions cancel exactly. An elementary radial identity exposes the cancellation, and evaluating closures with the same contact stress makes their coefficients directly comparable. Although superposition solves the bulk equation, it leaves a flux error on each shared contact. This error defines a unique finite-energy weak correction whose positive diffusive dissipation, suitably normalized, is a weak-energy coefficient. Explicit symmetric trials yield a variational lower bound and a residual upper bound, and exact integration with outward rational arithmetic proves that the weak-energy coefficient lies between 1.8266948 and 1.8267157. For the physical viscosity coefficient this is a conditional interval: the two coefficients coincide when the physical three-body correction equals the weak correction and the remote remainder of the pair adjoint identity, a surface term at large pair separation, vanishes. The interval excludes every closure coefficient compared here, including the zero of superposition. Hydrodynamic interactions contribute at the same orders in real suspensions, where rheometry measures total viscosities, so the coefficient is a quantitative benchmark for theories and simulations of dilute three-body Brownian stress in this model.
item.dc:creator: Julian Olszewski, Zijian Liu, Jie Xu

item.title: Phase Separation in a Mixture System of Active and Passive Particles
item.description: arXiv:2610.37193v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We carried out molecular dynamics simulations of a mixture of self-propelled particles (SPPs) and passive particles. When the self-propulsion speed was sufficiently high, the system separated into two phases. One phase consists of ordered passive particles, and the other is a disordered mixture of both particle types. The separation arises from the interplay between the self-propelled motion of SPPs and thermal motion of the passive particles, since phase separation does not appear with either particle type alone. As the self-propulsion speed increases, the SPPs push surrounding particles away, effectively increasing their excluded size. As a result, the increase in the effective excluded sizes promotes the accumulation of passive particles and the segregation of SPPs into the dilute phase through a mechanism analogous to the depletion interaction. This mechanism explains the phase separation observed in the present study. Our findings provide insights into the potential applications of SPPs and contribute to our understanding of natural systems composed of elements with different levels of motility.
item.dc:creator: Reo Arakaki, Tetsuya Hiraiwa, Ryo Akiyama

item.title: From OpenSPIM to FlowSPIM: Enhancing the versatility of a light-sheet microscope through an iterative design process
item.description: arXiv:2609.31115v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Light-sheet microscopy is ideal for the 3D imaging of large biological specimens, yet systematic documentation on adapting microscope designs to diverse experimental requirements remains limited. We present the iterative process used to design and build a modular light-sheet microscope and adapt it to different sample types and experimental conditions, including live and fixed zebrafish, Drosophila, and mouse gastruloids, as well as cellulose nanocrystals. Starting from a stripped-down OpenSPIM platform, we gradually made our microscope more versatile by adding hardware such as additional laser channels and optical filters, and new protocols for sample handling. In its final iteration, FlowSPIM is a new flow-based incubation technique for 3D tissue culture.
item.dc:creator: Endre Joachim Lerheim Mossige, Sergey Ponomartsev, Natalia Smirnova, Wietske van der Ent, Siri Andresen, Xian Hu, Felix Margadant, Rainer Heintzmann, Roland K\'ad\'ar, Kesavan Sekar, Helene Kn{\ae}velsrud, Camila Vicencio Esguerra, Stefan Krauss, Dag Kristian Dysthe, Alexander Refsum Jensenius

item.title: Before the First Bond: Depletion-Assisted Stochastic Capture at the Onset of Endocytosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.01321v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The first barrier to receptor-mediated endocytosis is not binding but arrival within a few nanometers of the membrane. In a crowded extracellular environment, this pre-contact approach is driven by thermal fluctuations and entropic depletion, yet continuum models usually start from established contact or treat the approach deterministically. We formulate a thermodynamically consistent stochastic theory for this stage. The sphere--plane depletion geometry uses the exact Asakura--Oosawa spherical-cap overlap, not a fitted cap, with either ideal van~'t~Hoff or pressure-only Carnahan--Starling (CS) pressure. Near-wall mobility enters with its essential and often omitted noise-induced drift. The first specific reaction is a Robin radiation boundary; the outer boundary is reflecting or absorbing. Three first-passage quantities are obtained analytically by quadrature: the mean reaction time, the reaction-before-escape probability, and the conditional success time, the last encoded by a Doob transform that exposes the selection bias of conditioning on capture. The local Damk\"ohler number diagnoses the boundary reaction-to-diffusion ratio, while the mean-time crossover follows from the exact reaction and diffusion terms. At baseline, ideal and CS contact depths are \(2.33\) and \(5.95\,k_{\rm B}T\), and the reflecting-outer mean reaction time is approximately \(0.20\,{\rm ms}\); with an absorbing outer boundary the conditional success time is shorter, but the two observables use different boundary protocols. Numerical checks reproduce the analytic results and the radiation-boundary mass balance. This provides a quantitative theoretical framework for crowding-assisted capture before membrane wrapping.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu
